explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The five kings fled and hid in the cave at Makkedah (Joshua 10:16). Five grown kings in one cave. I bet the last one in got the spot by the draft and had plenty to say about it.

Close, friend, but that's a different cave. David, who later became Israel's king, escaped to the cave of Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1). Here the five kings hide at Makkedah. Lots of caves in this land, so it's easy to mix them up.

That's a cave with a whole different story, friend. Abraham buried his wife Sarah in the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 23:19). The five kings hide in the cave at Makkedah. Same word 'cave,' very different day.

explanations.answer: Roll large stones against its mouth
explanations.explanation: That's it. Joshua says, "Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave, and post men there to guard them." The kings are found, and the cave becomes a shut door. Nobody walks out of there until Joshua says so.

explanations.answer: Dig a trench around its entrance
explanations.explanation: Nice try, baker, but nobody picks up a shovel here. The text has Joshua order large stones rolled against the mouth of the cave. He also has men posted there to guard it. Rolling stones is faster than digging, and I think everybody's glad about that.

explanations.answer: Light a fire at its entrance
explanations.explanation: No fire in this passage, friend. Joshua says to roll large stones against the mouth of the cave and to post men there to guard. That's the whole plan for the cave. I only know fire from my oven, and there I keep it pointed at cookies.

explanations.answer: Chase the enemy and attack from behind
explanations.explanation: Right on target. Joshua tells them, "But you, do not stop there. Pursue your enemies and attack them from behind." The cave is handled, so the rest of the men keep moving. Joshua doesn't want anybody standing around admiring the stones.

explanations.answer: Head back to camp and rest up
explanations.explanation: Not yet, baker. Joshua says, "But you, do not stop there," and sends the men after the enemy. The army does come back to the camp at Makkedah, but only after the chase is finished (Joshua 10:20-21). Rest comes later, and I bet it felt great.

explanations.answer: Gather the spoils from the field
explanations.explanation: Nothing about gathering anything in these verses, friend. Joshua's order is to pursue the enemies and attack them from behind. He also tells them not to let the enemy reach their cities. The job on the table is the chase.

That's the word. Joshua says, "Do not let them reach their cities, for the LORD your God has delivered them into your hand." The text then says the survivors retreated to the fortified cities (Joshua 10:20). So the cities are where the enemy was headed.

No boats in this one, baker. The word is cities. Joshua tells his men not to let the enemy reach their cities, because the LORD has delivered them into their hand. I only know ships from the bubbles in my dough, and those don't sail.

Tents are camp talk, friend, and that's where Israel's army ends up. Joshua's words are about the enemy's cities. He says, "Do not let them reach their cities." The survivors who got away did retreat to fortified cities (Joshua 10:20).

I see why you'd think so after a fight like that, but the text says otherwise. "The whole army returned safely to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah." Safely is the word. The army comes back to camp whole.

Yes, baker, it's false. The text says, "The whole army returned safely to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah." No lost men are mentioned. I'd say that's good news for the camp, and a lot of people probably counted heads twice.
That's right. The text says, "…no one dared to utter a word against the Israelites." After that chase, the whole land goes quiet. Not even a grumble came out.

It's true, friend. Joshua 10:21 says "…no one dared to utter a word against the Israelites." Nobody spoke up against them. I'd have kept my mouth shut too, and I'm a stamper with a mustache for hands.

Yes, baker. Joshua summons all the men of Israel, then speaks to the army commanders who had come with him. They step up and put their feet on the necks of the kings (Joshua 10:24). Everybody is watching, so the whole army sees it.

The Levites don't show up here, friend. The text says Joshua spoke to the army commanders who had accompanied him. Those commanders came forward and put their feet on the kings' necks. This scene belongs to the commanders.

The Gibeonites are the people of Gibeon, the city the five kings had gone to war against (Joshua 10:5). They aren't in this scene, baker. Joshua tells the army commanders who came with him to put their feet on the kings' necks. Gibeon is where this whole story began, so it's easy to keep them in mind.

explanations.answer: The LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Joshua says, "Do not be afraid or discouraged… Be strong and courageous, for the LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight." His reason is the LORD, and nothing else. The courage comes from who is fighting with them.

explanations.answer: The rest of the kings have already given up
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. Joshua gives one reason: "…the LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight." In fact, he says they will keep fighting enemies. The courage rests on the LORD, not on enemies quitting.

explanations.answer: Their army is bigger than any in the land
explanations.explanation: Joshua never says anything about army size, baker. His words are, "Be strong and courageous, for the LORD will do this to all the enemies you fight." The reason is the LORD. Counting heads is not part of his speech.

The text says something different, friend. Joshua hung the bodies on five trees and left them there until evening. At sunset he ordered them taken down (Joshua 10:26-27). This is a heavy part of the story, and I think it's okay to feel that.

Right, it's false. The text says Joshua left the bodies on the trees "until evening." Then "at sunset Joshua ordered that they be taken down from the trees." This is a heavy part, baker, so I'll just say it plainly and move on.

explanations.answer: They were still there when this was written
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says the stones are there "to this day." The writer tells us the stones were still at the mouth of that cave when it was written. They were set in place at Joshua's order, and the text says they stayed.

explanations.answer: They were rolled away a few years later
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says, friend. It says large stones were placed against the mouth of the cave, "and the stones are there to this day." No rolling away is mentioned. The writer points to them as still sitting there.

explanations.answer: They were carried off to build an altar
explanations.explanation: No altar in this verse, baker. The text just says the stones were placed at the cave's mouth, "and the stones are there to this day." Nobody carries them off. They stay put, and I think they're good at it.

explanations.answer: The LORD the God of Israel
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says Joshua did this "just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded." This is a heavy part of the story, and I think it's okay to feel that. The writer wants us to see that the command came from the LORD and not from Joshua's own idea.

The elders aren't named here, friend. The text says Joshua did this "just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded." That is the one who gave the command. It's a heavy verse, so I'll stay plain about it.

The priests aren't named in this verse, baker. The text says it was "just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had commanded." The command comes from the LORD Himself. This is a heavy part, so I'll keep it simple.

I get why it feels like a long list of cities, but the text says one campaign. "…Joshua captured all these kings and their land in one campaign." That's the verse, baker. One campaign covers all of it.
Yes, it's false. Joshua 10:42 says he "captured all these kings and their land in one campaign." That's a lot of cities in one trip. I can barely finish one batch before the timer goes off.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD fought for Israel
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says, "…because the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel, Joshua captured all these kings and their land in one campaign." The reason is the LORD. That matches what Joshua told his commanders earlier about being strong and courageous.

The text never says anything about numbers, friend. It gives one reason: "…because the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel." The win comes from the LORD fighting for Israel. No head count is mentioned.

explanations.answer: Because the kings had no city walls
explanations.explanation: The text points the other way, baker. The survivors retreated to the fortified cities (Joshua 10:20). The reason given for the win is that "the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel." Walls or no walls, that's what the text says.

That's right. The passage ends with, "Then Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal." The campaign is done, and everyone goes back to camp. I think it was a good night's sleep for the whole bunch.
It's true, friend. Joshua 10:43 says, "Then Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal." That's where this chapter ends. Gilgal is the camp, so there's your answer.
